note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Question a, wording: The right option is the only one with a hedge ('mostly') and repeats the remember line almost word for word. Two distractors use absolutes ('all inland', 'none inland… none on the coast'), so a student can pick the answer by eliminating extremes without knowing the idea.

rejected.title: Comparing Australia and the United States
card: Australia has a small number of very large cities. Most of them are capital cities on or near the coast, such as Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane.
The United States has many large cities spread across the whole country. Some are on the coasts, such as New York and Los Angeles. Others are inland, such as Chicago and Denver.

Both countries have a large share of their people living in cities. The difference is the pattern: Australia's urban population is concentrated in a few places, while the United States has a wider spread.
Inland Australia has few large cities, so many people there live in small towns or on farms and stations. The United States has big inland cities as well as coastal ones.
rejected.remember: Australia has few big cities, mostly coastal. The United States has many, spread across the country.

a.q: Which statement best compares the large cities of Australia and the United States?
opts: Australia has few, mostly coastal. The US has many, spread
Australia has many, spread out. The US has few, coastal
Australia has none inland. The US has none on the coast
Australia has more large cities than the US, all inland
a.why: Australia's big cities are few and mostly coastal, while the United States has many across the country, including inland. The reversed option is wrong because it swaps the two countries.
a.clue: Think about how many big cities each country has and where they are.

b.q: Ella marks the ten largest cities of Australia and of the United States on two maps. What pattern is she most likely to see?
opts: US: inland and coastal. Australia: mostly coastal
US: mostly coastal. Australia: inland and coastal
Both: mostly coastal, with few inland cities
Both: spread evenly across the inland and coast
b.why: The United States has large cities on its coasts and inland, such as Chicago and Denver, while Australia's largest cities are mostly on or near the coast. The option saying both are mostly coastal is wrong because it ignores the big inland cities of the United States.
b.clue: Which country has big cities far from the sea?

problems.detail: 'Inland Australia has few large cities, so people there live in small towns or on farms and stations' implies all inland Australians live in small towns or on properties. Canberra (about 470,000 people) and regional cities such as Toowoomba, Ballarat, Bendigo and Wagga Wagga are inland. Suggested fix: 'many people there live in small towns or on farms and stations.'

The stem already says Chicago and Denver are 'large cities far from the coast', so the right option ('spread inland as well as on the coast') largely restates the stem. A student could pick it without understanding the comparison with Australia.
Why (b) says the coastal option is wrong partly 'because ... Australia's big cities are mostly coastal'. That clause is irrelevant to why the US option is wrong and could confuse students.

check.summary: Both intended answers are correct and unambiguous. The card overgeneralises that inland Australians live in small towns or on farms, ignoring Canberra and inland regional cities. Question b's stem nearly gives away its answer, and why (b) includes an irrelevant clause about Australia.
